title: Jimmy Maxwell and the Ellington band at the Rainbow Grill
summary: Jimmy Maxwell, a friend of Cootie, admires his playing; Baron describes the post-Duke band and the album The Unknown Sessions.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Here’s what — remember Jimmy Maxwell, the trumpet player?

He played with Benny Goodman. I know he played with Mercer. But I can’t remember, but he was dear friends with Cootie. We were like, one time, right after Duke passed, he came out with the band and there was like this like two week engagement in Bermuda and they were flying people in. Like Ella was there and Billy Taylor, all kinds of people. So they were flying in and everything worked out. So Jimmy Maxwell played in some rehearsal bands that I was in, and we got to be really good friends. And he used to say, “Man you sound more like Tricky Sam Nanton, than Tricky Sam. And even at that time I didn’t even know how to — he just loved my playing. I loved playing with him. Playing

in small groups with him and stuff. So the band, Duke’s band was playing at the Rainbow Grill from like Monday or Tuesday to Saturday. Sunday nights they didn’t play. But that band was sax section, trumpet, and rhythm section. They used the same charts. And somehow, his music is so heavy that it’s just worked. They know how to play it. Did you ever hear the album “The Unknown Sessions?”

Oh find that. It’s four horns. It’s like alto — Harry and Johnny, alto and bari; Ray Nance, Lawrence Brown. That’s a common combination. It’s on CD now for sure. And like you know the alto is here and the baritone is here, and it still sounds like a sax section.
That’s right, you know the right tessitura, the right part of the instrument, and so anyway, I keep going on these tangents, so Jimmy — you don’t mind, do you? —
